segments.narration: Fifty stone terraces vanished in a single night. Lake Rotomahana, New Zealand, the tenth of June 1886. Mount Tarawera tore open a seventeen-kilometre rift.
Before that, the Pink and White Terraces were the country's great attraction. Silica staircases, dropping twenty-five metres over fifty basins of warm water.
Victorians sailed the world to bathe there. Then the crater filled and the lake rose thirty to forty metres. Where exactly had the terraces been?
In 2010 an archivist in Basel opened Ferdinand von Hochstetter's 1859 survey diary. His bearings were the last accurate fix on the lost shoreline.
Two teams read it differently: buried under the shore, or drowned by the new lake. The latest reconstruction, diary plus lidar, puts them underwater.

verdicts.claim: Mount Tarawera erupted on 10 June 1886, opening a 17 km rift across the mountain and Lake Rotomahana and destroying the Pink and White Terraces.
verdicts.note: 86% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 3 number(s)

verdicts.claim: The White Terraces covered about 8 hectares in roughly 50 layers descending about 25 m, and the terraces were New Zealand's most famous tourist attraction.
verdicts.note: 86% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 3 number(s)

verdicts.claim: The eruption left a crater more than 100 m deep that filled with water, forming a lake 30 to 40 m higher than the old one.
verdicts.note: 86% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 3 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Ferdinand von Hochstetter's 1859 survey is considered the most accurate record of the pre-eruption lake, and his field diary was found in the Hochstetter Collection Basel when Sascha Nolden took up its curation in 2010.
verdicts.note: 87% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Bunn and Nolden's 2017 paper placed the terraces buried 10 to 15 m underground near the shoreline, while GNS Science, Bill Keir and a later NIWA reconstruction using the diary and lidar place the former sites beneath the modern lake.
verdicts.note: 81% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 3 number(s)
